title: How do you securely manage secrets (DB passwords, cloud keys, JWT secrets) in a CI/CD pipeline (secret stores/Vault/cloud secret managers, masked variables — never committed or baked into images)?
shortTitle: Securely Managing Secrets in a CI/CD Pipeline

s1_definition.profdef: Managing secrets in a CI/CD pipeline means keeping sensitive values such as database passwords, cloud access keys, and JWT signing keys out of source code, out of build logs, and out of built images, and instead fetching them at runtime from a dedicated secret store. The core practices are: store secrets in a purpose-built manager such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or the CI system's encrypted secret store; inject them as masked environment variables or mounted files only for the step that needs them; never commit them to Git and never bake them into a Docker image layer; prefer short-lived, dynamically issued credentials over long-lived static keys; and rotate and audit access centrally.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's vault keys. You would never write the vault combination on the branch noticeboard (source code), print it on every delivered parcel (image layer), or read it aloud over the intercom (build logs). Instead the combination lives in a central key-management office (the secret store). When a teller needs it for one transaction, the office hands over a temporary code that works for a few minutes and then expires (short-lived credentials), the teller uses it quietly (masked at runtime), and the office keeps a log of exactly who asked and when (audit). The key is never copied, never printed, and never left lying around.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep secrets out of code, logs, and images; fetch them at runtime from a dedicated secret store as masked variables or mounted files; and prefer short-lived, rotated, audited credentials over static keys.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Managing secrets in a CI/CD pipeline means keeping sensitive values such as database passwords, cloud access keys, and JWT signing keys out of source code, out of build logs, and out of built images, and instead fetching them at runtime from a dedicated secret store. The core practices are: store secrets in a purpose-built manager such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or the CI system's encrypted secret store; inject them as masked environment variables or mounted files only for the step that needs them; never commit them to Git and never bake them into a Docker image layer; prefer short-lived, dynamically issued credentials over long-lived static keys; and rotate and audit access centrally.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's vault keys. You would never write the vault combination on the branch noticeboard (source code), print it on every delivered parcel (image layer), or read it aloud over the intercom (build logs). Instead the combination lives in a central key-management office (the secret store). When a teller needs it for one transaction, the office hands over a temporary code that works for a few minutes and then expires (short-lived credentials), the teller uses it quietly (masked at runtime), and the office keeps a log of exactly who asked and when (audit). The key is never copied, never printed, and never left lying around.

**One line to remember:** Keep secrets out of code, logs, and images; fetch them at runtime from a dedicated secret store as masked variables or mounted files; and prefer short-lived, rotated, audited credentials over static keys.

sections.s2_technical:
The first rule is that secrets never live in Git. No passwords in `application.yml`, no cloud keys in a committed `.env`, no JWT secret in a properties file. Instead the repo contains only references, such as a placeholder `${DB_PASSWORD}` that is resolved at runtime. A pre-commit secret scanner (like gitleaks or truffleHog) is wired into CI to fail the build if a secret is ever accidentally committed, because once a secret is in Git history it is considered compromised and must be rotated.

The second rule is that secrets never get baked into images. A common mistake is `ENV DB_PASSWORD=...` or copying a secrets file into the image during `docker build`, because every image layer is readable by anyone who can pull the image, and the value persists forever in the registry. Instead the image contains only code, and the secret is provided at container start as an environment variable or a mounted file from the orchestrator.

Secrets come from a dedicated store. HashiCorp Vault issues secrets and can generate dynamic, short-lived database credentials on demand that auto-expire. Cloud-native managers like AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, or GCP Secret Manager, store and rotate secrets with IAM-controlled access. The CI system also has an encrypted store: GitHub Actions encrypted secrets, GitLab CI masked and protected variables, or the Jenkins credentials store. The pipeline reads from one of these at the moment of use.

Injection is scoped and masked. A pipeline references a secret by name and the CI system injects it as an environment variable for only the step that needs it, automatically masking it in logs so it prints as `***`. For example a deploy step reads a registry password from the credential store to push an image, but the password never appears in the console. In Kubernetes the running application reads secrets from a mounted Kubernetes Secret or, better, from an external secret synced in by the External Secrets Operator or Vault Agent, so the cluster pulls the value from the real store rather than storing it long-term.

Prefer short-lived over static. The strongest pattern is no static secret at all: the CI job authenticates to the cloud using OpenID Connect federation, so GitHub Actions exchanges a signed identity token for temporary cloud credentials that last minutes, and there is no long-lived access key to leak. Similarly, a service in Kubernetes uses a workload identity or an IAM role rather than an embedded key. When a static secret is unavoidable, it must be rotated on a schedule and immediately if exposed.

A senior nuance is blast-radius and least privilege: each pipeline and each environment gets its own narrowly scoped credentials, so a leaked QA credential cannot touch Prod, and a leaked registry-read token cannot delete anything. Another nuance is auditability, which banks require: the secret store logs every access, so you can answer who read the production database password and when. A third nuance is defence against log leakage: masking is best-effort, so you also avoid echoing secrets, disable verbose command tracing for secret-handling steps, and treat any secret that might have hit a log as compromised and rotate it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An engineer at the National Bank of India once committed the production database password into application.yml "just to test," and it sat in Git history for weeks. Anyone with repo access, including a contractor, could read it. This is exactly the problem a secret store plus commit scanning solves. The password lives only in the store, the repo holds a placeholder, and a scanner fails the build if a secret is ever committed.

Problem 2 — A Dockerfile baked a cloud access key into an ENV line, so the key was readable in every pulled image layer and persisted in the registry. This is exactly the problem runtime injection solves. The image holds only code, and the key is provided at container start from the secret store, never in a layer.

Problem 3 — The team could not answer an auditor's question of who read the production DB password and when. This is exactly the problem a centralised, audited store with short-lived credentials solves. Every access is logged, and credentials are short-lived so a leak expires quickly.

To make this concrete without a real Vault we will write a Java simulation of secure secret handling. We will model a `SecretStore` that issues short-lived, audited secrets by name, a `Pipeline` step that fetches a secret at runtime and masks it in logs, and an `ImageBuilder` that refuses to bake secrets into the image. We will show a deploy step fetching a masked DB password and a registry token, show the audit log of accesses, and show the image builder rejecting an attempt to embed a secret. This mirrors real secret-store-backed, masked, never-baked secret management.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it
java -cp target/classes com.bank.secrets.SecretsDemo

# Real usage: scan for accidentally committed secrets before every push
gitleaks detect --source . --no-banner
# Secrets are read at runtime from the store, e.g.:
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/db-password --query SecretString --output text
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a secret store preloaded with a Prod DB password and a registry token, plus a deploy step and two image-build attempts.

Step 1: The store is loaded with two secrets by name. These are the only place the real values live; the repo and images will never contain them.

Step 2: The deploy step runs. It fetches the DB password and the registry token from the store at the moment of use. The store issues short-lived copies with a five-minute TTL and records each access in its audit log with the caller name and timestamp.

Step 3: The deploy step uses the secrets to log in to the registry and create a Kubernetes secret, but it logs through the masking logger, so the actual values are replaced with `***` and never appear in plain text. The secrets then go out of scope and are not persisted anywhere.

Step 4: The audit log is printed, showing exactly that the deploy step read the DB password and the registry token and when, which is the record an auditor needs.

Step 5: The first image build attempt includes an ENV line embedding the DB password. The image builder detects the secret-looking ENV and throws a SecurityException, refusing to bake the secret into a layer.

Step 6: The second image build attempt contains only the base image and the application JAR, so it succeeds, producing a clean image whose secrets will be injected at runtime rather than stored in a layer.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Git repo: placeholder ${DB_PASSWORD}  ← NO real secret
  Dockerfile: code only                 ← NO real secret
    │
    ▼ pipeline deploy step (runtime)
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │   SecretStore (Vault/SM)      │  ← real values + audit log
  │   issue("prod/db-password")   │
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ short-lived (5 min TTL)
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │   PipelineStep                │  use secret
  │   MaskingLogger → prints ***  │  ← never plain text in logs
  └──────────────┬────────────────┘
                 ▼
  docker login / kubectl create secret  (secret used, then out of scope)

  ImageBuilder: ENV with PASSWORD/KEY/TOKEN → SecurityException (rejected)
  Audit: store records WHO read WHICH secret WHEN
```

```
  │ + put(name,value)        │        │ + value(): String        │
  │ + issue(name,caller)     │        │ + isExpired(): boolean   │

   ┌──────────┴───────────┐

  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ PipelineStep │  │  MaskingLogger   │
  │ + deploy()   │─▶│ + info(msg,secret)│ redacts value → ***
  └──────────────┘  └──────────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     ImageBuilder         │
  │ + build(lines)           │ throws SecurityException on secret ENV
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Secret Lifecycle ───────────────────────

  [IN_STORE] → issue() → [SHORT_LIVED_IN_USE] → out of scope → [DISCARDED]
       │                        │ TTL elapses
       │                        ▼
       └── rotate on schedule   [EXPIRED]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. step.deploy()
  2.   → store.issue("prod/db-password","deploy-step") → audit + Secret(ttl=300)
  3.   → store.issue("prod/registry-token","deploy-step")
  4.   → maskLog.info("... " + token.value(), token) → prints "... ***"
  5. imageBuilder.build(linesWithEnvSecret) → SecurityException
  6. imageBuilder.build(cleanLines) → OK
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Managing secrets in a CI/CD pipeline comes down to keeping sensitive values out of three places where they tend to leak, and fetching them from one place where they are safe. The three places they must never appear are source code, build logs, and image layers. The one place they live is a dedicated secret store such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or the CI system's encrypted secret store. The repository holds only placeholders, and the pipeline resolves the real values at runtime from the store.

Concretely, I never commit secrets to Git, and I wire a secret scanner like gitleaks into CI so the build fails if one is ever committed, because once a secret is in Git history it is compromised and must be rotated. I never bake secrets into images, because every image layer is readable by anyone who can pull it and persists forever in the registry; the image carries only code, and the secret is injected at container start as a masked environment variable or a mounted file. When the pipeline does use a secret, it references it by name, the CI system injects it only for that step and masks it in logs so it prints as stars, and in Kubernetes the running app reads it from an external secret synced from the real store.

The strongest pattern is having no static secret at all. The pipeline authenticates to the cloud with OpenID Connect federation, exchanging a signed identity token for temporary credentials that last only minutes, so there is no long-lived access key to leak. Where a static secret is unavoidable, it is scoped with least privilege per environment and rotated on a schedule.

On the banking project I moved us from a disaster, where someone had committed the production database password into application.yml and baked a cloud key into a Dockerfile ENV, to a clean model: the repo held placeholders, images held only code, the deploy pipeline fetched the DB password and registry token from the secret store at runtime with everything masked in logs, and we used OIDC so there were no stored cloud keys. The senior points I always add are least privilege so a leaked QA credential can never touch Prod, full audit logging in the store so we can answer exactly who read the production password and when, which an auditor always asks, and treating any secret that might have touched a log as compromised and rotating it immediately.
